opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think domain experts are really important, especially at the stage where you're trying to define what "good" even looks like. When we started working on deep research, one of the first things we had to figure out was: what does a great research report look like in finance, versus in medicine, versus in, say, policy or engineering? And the honest answer is that those standards are pretty different, and people like me aren't qualified to judge all of them.

So a big part of the work was bringing in people who actually do this kind of research for a living and having them help create tasks that reflect the real questions they'd want answered. That might be an analyst who'd normally spend hours pulling together information on a company, or a doctor trying to synthesize the literature on a particular treatment. They know which sources are trustworthy, what a lazy answer looks like, and what details actually matter versus what just sounds impressive.

That said, you can't hire an expert for every niche in the world, so the hope is that the model learns more general skills from that data: how to search, how to backtrack when it hits a dead end, how to weigh conflicting sources, how to synthesize. If you get enough coverage across a diverse set of domains, those behaviors transfer, and the model gets good at research in areas it was never explicitly trained on.

Experts are also really valuable for evaluation. It's easy to be fooled by a long, well-formatted report, so having people with real expertise read outputs and tell you "this is subtly wrong" or "this missed the key paper" is one of the most useful signals you can get. So I'd say they're essential both for shaping the training data and for keeping us honest about whether the model is actually getting better.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so domain experts have been really important for us, and I think the way we use them is maybe a little different from what people expect. We're not really using them to teach the model facts about a field. The model already knows a lot. What we actually need from them is a sense of what a good answer looks like in their domain, and what a bad answer looks like, and that turns out to be surprisingly hard to specify.

So for deep research, we'd work with people in, say, finance or biology or law, and we'd ask them to write the kind of tasks they'd actually give to a junior analyst or a grad student. Real tasks, not toy ones. And then the more valuable part is having them look at the outputs and tell us where it falls short. Often it's things that are very obvious to an expert and completely invisible to us. Like, the model cited a source that someone in the field would never trust, or it treated two things as equivalent that an expert knows are not, or it did a lot of work but missed the one thing that actually mattered for the question.

And then our job is to turn that into something the model can learn from. Sometimes that's rubrics, sometimes it's examples, sometimes it's just changing how we think about the reward. The experts are giving us the taste, basically, and we're trying to generalize it.

The other thing I'd say is that you want breadth more than depth from any single person. We don't need the world's best oncologist. We need enough people across enough fields that the model learns the general skill of doing careful research, rather than memorizing what one person cares about. Because the thing we actually want is for it to do well on fields we never collected data for. And the encouraging thing is that it does seem to transfer. If you teach it to be rigorous about sourcing in a few domains, it gets better at that pretty broadly.

astra-6.text:
I think domain experts are really important because they can tell you what good research actually looks like in their field. It’s not just whether the final answer is correct. Did you ask the right question? Did you find the relevant evidence? Did you notice when two sources disagreed, and did you handle that disagreement well?

Those things can be hard to judge if you don’t have expertise. An answer might sound convincing to me, but someone who works in that area will immediately see that it missed a key assumption or relied on the wrong source.

The challenge is taking that feedback and teaching the model something that generalizes. You want it to learn how to evaluate evidence, recognize gaps, and know when it needs to investigate further. Then experts across different fields can help you understand where those general research skills work and where you need more specialized knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think domain experts are really important for helping us understand what good research actually looks like in a field. It’s relatively easy to evaluate whether a model got a factual question right. It’s much harder to evaluate whether it asked an interesting question, chose an appropriate method, or interpreted a result carefully. Those are places where expert judgment matters a lot.

And I think you want experts involved throughout the process, not just grading the final answer. They can help design tasks, identify where the model’s reasoning went wrong, and distinguish a useful contribution from something that just sounds sophisticated.

The challenge is turning that feedback into capabilities that generalize. You don’t want the model to just learn one expert’s preferred approach to a narrow problem. You want it to learn how to test assumptions, work with evidence, and recognize when it needs more information, while still respecting the different standards that different fields have.
